title: Cadillac Records
full_review:
"Cadillac Records" (Sony Music/Parkwood) is the colorful, sometimes sordid chronicle of the rise of the Chicago-based, rhythm-and-blues label Chess Records throughout the 1950s and 1960s.

The film traces how, with scant resources, owner Leonard Chess (Adrian Brody), a Polish emigre, assembles a legendary array of musicians starting with blues guitar prodigy Muddy Waters (Jeffrey Wright) and harmonica player Little Walter (Columbus Short). Eventually, the roster comes to include songwriter Big Willie Dixon (Cedric the Entertainer) and hulking Howlin' Wolf (Eamonn Walker).

In the 1950s, Chuck Berry (Mos Def) helps lead the label's "crossover" to mainstream audiences. But when he's suddenly arrested for transporting a minor across state lines, the crossover mantle falls to feisty Etta James (Beyonce Knowles, who is executive producer of the film).

Along with the professional successes and setbacks, the group's personal travails are also portrayed. Waters' loyal girlfriend, Geneva (Gabrielle Union), wards off Little Walter's forlorn affection, and copes with Muddy's numerous infidelities.

James arrives filled with anger and insecurities stemming from her being born out of wedlock to a prostitute mother and (so she was told) pool shark Minnesota Fats. Chess supports her through these emotional and drug-related problems, and though he is married to Revetta (Emmanuelle Chriqui) falls for her himself.

The relationship between Chess and his artists is a complex one. He's generally paternal and nurturing -- buying each one a Cadillac when they get their first gold record. But he's less than scrupulous with his bookkeeping and bribes radio stations to play his music.

Racial tensions often surface, as when Little Walter sasses a white policeman and takes a brutal beating in return and when Berry arrives for a local gig only to be rebuffed when the bigoted managers discover he's not a white country singer.

Also, the pilfering of R & B material by white performers -- Chuck Berry's "Sweet Little Sixteen" was appropriated almost note for note by the Beach Boys, for example -- became a regrettable problem as R & B morphed into rock 'n' roll and attracted a growing white teenage audience.

Writer-director Darnell Martin keeps the multiple plot strands reasonably comprehensible and evokes the tumultuous era convincingly.

Predictably, there's a flavorful earful of tunes, all but one (Little Walter's "Last Night I Lost a Friend") performed by the actors themselves. Knowles, transformed with her blonde wig and a few extra pounds, sounds marvelous in her numbers, including the smooth standard "At Last" and probably delivers her best screen performance to date. But the entire cast is excellent.

Some of the elements below may limit its appeal to Catholic viewers, but for rhythm-and-blues fans, "Cadillac Records" is a most interesting piece of music history.

The film contains pervasive rough language and some profanity; some brief nongraphic sexual encounters; some nonmarital, implied underage sex; innuendo; some racial violence; drug use and infidelity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
